extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of political theory, historians, and policymakers interested in comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observable signs for assessing the character, tendencies, and effects of democratic (vs. monarchical/aristocratic) regimes, especially regarding administration, magistrates' power, and public finance. Draws on historical examples and practical indicators (salaries, records, legislation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration of public officers as an index of regime change
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of paid for unpaid functionaries is of itself... sufficient to constitute a serious revolution. When a democratic republic renders offices which had formerly been remunerated gratuitous, the State is advancing to monarchical institutions; and when a monarchy begins to remunerate such officers as had hitherto been unpaid, it is a sure sign that it is approaching toward a despotic or a republican form of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whether offices are paid or gratuitous to infer tendencies: the presence or absence of gratuitous functionaries is a prominent sign of democratic dominion. Track changes from unpaid→paid or paid→unpaid as indicators of movement toward monarchy/despotism or toward republicanism respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform public remuneration and accessibility of office
rubrics_metrics.description: If public officers are not uniformly remunerated by the State, the public charges must be entrusted to men of opulence and independence... and if the people still retains its right of election, that election can only be made from a certain class of citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether remuneration practices restrict candidate pools to wealthy classes. If offices require private wealth to serve, the effect is aristocratic even under elective forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of arbitrary power exercised by magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: In two different kinds of government the magistrates exercise a considerable degree of arbitrary power; namely, under the absolute government of a single individual, and under that of a democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure how much discretion magistrates have (how much the law merely 'points out the object' and leaves means to them). Examples: New England selectmen drawing jury lists and forbidding liquor to habitual drunkards—powers that would be 'revolting' in other systems but are accepted in democratic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of elective franchise and short terms on magistrates' freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Nowhere has so much been left by the law to the arbitrary determination of the magistrate as in democratic republics... the freedom of the magistrate increases as the elective franchise is extended, and as the duration of the time of office is shortened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional features: breadth of suffrage and length of office terms. Broader franchise and shorter terms tend to increase officials' discretionary behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and continuity of administration (archives and records)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public administration is, so to speak, oral and traditionary. But little is committed to writing, and that little is wafted away forever... The only historical remains in the United States are the newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence of written records, archives, and institutional memory as indicators of administrative maturity. Instability (frequent turnover, lack of archives) prejudices the 'art of government' and hinders cumulative administrative learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social class composition and its impact on public finance
rubrics_metrics.description: The people may always be mentally divided into three distinct classes... The first consists of the wealthy; the second, of those in easy circumstances; and the third is composed of those who have little or no property... each of these classes will exercise an influence peculiar to its own propensities upon the administration of the finances of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who holds legislative power (wealthy, middle, poor) to predict spending/taxation patterns: middle-class governments tend to be most economical; rule by poorest classes tends to raise public expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of democracies to increase public expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the poor should be exclusively invested with the power of making the laws no great economy of public expenditure ought to be expected: that expenditure will always be considerable... the government of the democracy is the only one under which the power which lays on taxes escapes the payment of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use electorate composition to anticipate pressures for redistribution, public relief, and public amusements; democracies with poor majorities likely favor higher public spending benefiting the majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property ownership moderates democratic extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: The extravagance of democracy is, however, less to be dreaded in proportion as the people acquires a share of property... America, where the great majority of the citizens possess some fortune, is in a still more favorable position than France.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate distribution of property: broader property ownership among the electorate reduces incentive and opportunity for excessive taxation/spending targeted at the poor majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic appetite for multitudinous improvements and innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: A thousand different objects are subjected to improvement; the most trivial details are sought out as susceptible of amendment; and those changes which are accompanied with considerable expense are more especially advocated... all democratic communities are agitated by an ill-defined excitement and by a kind of feverish impatience, that engender a multitude of innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for rapid policy churn, many small costly reforms, and popular impatience as hallmarks of democratic governance that can raise expenditure and administrative burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of administrative continuity causing waste
rubrics_metrics.description: As the designs which it entertains are frequently changed, and the agents of those designs are still more frequently removed, its undertakings are often ill conducted or left unfinished: in the former case the State spends sums out of all proportion to the end which it proposes to accomplish; in the second, the expense itself is unprofitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use turnover rates and project completion statistics to estimate inefficiency/waste: frequent personnel change correlates with poorly executed or abandoned projects and disproportionate expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of public salaries under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic State is most parsimonious towards its principal agents. In America the secondary officers are much better paid, and the dignitaries of the administration much worse, than they are elsewhere... the scale of remuneration is determined by the consideration of its own wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare salary scales across rank: democracies tend to raise pay for subordinate officers (closer to people) while keeping principal officers' salaries low; use salary tables (e.g., U.S. Treasury example) as diagnostic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/moral habits of a people influence public spending independently of institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Independently of the laws, all these causes concur to exercise a very powerful influence upon the conduct of the finances of the State... If the Americans never spend the money of the people in galas, it is not only because the imposition of taxes is under the control of the people, but because the people takes no delight in public rejoicings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish effects due to institutional arrangements from those due to national tastes, commercial character, or cultural values when assessing fiscal behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for reliable statistical bases to compare national expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to estimate the amount of the public charges of a people two preliminaries are indispensable: it is necessary... to know the wealth of that people; and... to learn what portion of that wealth is devoted to the expenditure of the State... The wealth of nations is composed of population, real property, and personal property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing public expenditure across countries, require comprehensive data on population, real property, and personal property; absence of county/township accounts (as in the U.S. case) undermines accurate cross-national comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative delegates tend to conform to constituents' passions
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be believed that the delegate will in the end conform to the principles of his constituents, and favor their propensities as much as their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use responsiveness of representatives to popular preference as predictor of policy orientation; even with imperfect representation, delegates often echo constituent demands, affecting fiscal and regulatory choices.
